gaps: The candidate never addresses the Lobby view (create-table with blinds, join-by-table_id+seat+name+buy-in) that the reference explicitly calls out as View 1 — the candidate's scope statement narrows to the table/game view only and the omission is never flagged as deliberately out of scope, leaving 'how does a player ever get to a seat' unresolved for a later stage.

The candidate specifies no concrete implementation stack at all (framework or no framework, build step or none, language) — the reference commits to a specific, justified minimal stack (static index.html/app.js/style.css, fetch + native WebSocket, no dependency). This is a legitimate free choice to differ, but the candidate doesn't make any choice, concrete or alternative, leaving tech-stack selection to be resolved unilaterally by a later stage.

The reference's simple table-layout convention (oval/circle of seats around a center pot/board area) that makes 'whose turn' and 'who's the button' legible at a glance is not described in the candidate — the candidate covers the acting-seat highlight and button data (buttonSeat) but never specifies the actual visual layout that would make those readable.
superior_choices: The candidate's actionSeq/handSeq gap-detection protocol (compare event.actionSeq to TableView.actionSeq+1, and handSeq continuity, then set DESYNCED and issue REQUEST_SYNC) is a materially more rigorous state-sync mechanism than the reference's blanket 'every message replaces state wholesale' — it gives two independent implementers a precise, testable trigger for when a resync is required versus when incremental application is safe, rather than relying on 'always full snapshot' as the only correctness guarantee.

The optimistic-UI submission flow (fresh actionId, pendingAction tracking, explicit non-optimistic treatment of game-state numbers vs. optimistic treatment of only the 'in flight' UI state, idempotent resend safety via actionId, a distinct client-side UI timeout shorter than the server's actionTimeoutMs) is considerably more detailed and implementation-ready than the reference's brief 'apply response body immediately, WS push is idempotent' treatment.

The hole-card privacy section is unusually thorough: it explicitly enumerates the one legitimate exception (SHOWDOWN.revealedHands for non-folded seats), states the invariant that no in-memory client structure ever holds a non-self Card value outside that exception, and explains why fold-then-next-hand transitions can't leak stale cards — going beyond the reference's more general 'client can't leak what it was never given' framing with concrete implementation guarantees.

Section 3.3 makes the UX-vs-enforcement boundary an explicit, load-bearing statement ('the action panel is not the enforcement mechanism'), including the adversarial framing (a compromised/hand-edited client can only ever get ACTION_REJECTED) — this is present only implicitly in the reference's action-submission section.

The integration-contract summary table in §7 is a strong cross-document consistency aid that the reference lacks — it makes every client behavior traceable to a specific server guarantee/section, reducing the risk of drift between the two documents at a later implementation stage.
summary: The candidate is a technically deeper and more implementation-ready document than the reference in the areas it covers: its actionSeq/handSeq gap-detection-and-resync protocol is a materially sounder state-sync mechanism than the reference's blanket full-replace approach, its optimistic-UI/action-submission flow is more precisely specified (idempotent actionId, distinct client-side timeout, explicit no-optimistic-game-state-update rule), and its hole-card privacy treatment is exceptionally thorough, including the showdown-reveal exception and an explicit no-leak invariant. It is also fully internally consistent, with a useful closing integration-contract table cross-referencing every client behavior to its server guarantee. However, it is scoped narrower than the reference: it entirely omits the Lobby view (table creation/join flow) that the reference treats as a first-class view, and it never commits to any concrete implementation stack (framework/build-step/language), leaving that decision unresolved for a later stage where the reference makes a deliberate, justified choice (static HTML/JS, no framework). These are real completeness gaps, but they sit alongside genuinely superior mechanism design in the harder, more safety-critical parts of the client (sync correctness, action idempotency, privacy invariants).
